What is the biological process of sourdough fermentation?
a: A sourdough starter is a naturally occurring culture of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria that work together to ferment dough. When flour and water are mixed, naturally occurring yeast (primarily Saccharomyces exiguus) and lactic acid bacteria (primarily Lactobacillus sanfranciscensis) begin to grow. The yeast consumes sugars in the flour, producing carbon dioxide and alcohol through alcoholic fermentation. The carbon dioxide is what causes the dough to rise. Meanwhile, the lactic acid bacteria consume the same sugars and produce lactic and acetic acids as metabolic byproducts, which give sourdough its characteristic tangy flavor. The bacteria also lower the pH of the dough, creating an acidic environment that inhibits the growth of harmful microorganisms while favoring the beneficial yeast and bacteria. This symbiotic relationship is self-sustaining — as long as the starter is regularly fed with fresh flour and water, the microbial community continues to thrive. The balance between yeast and bacteria can be influenced by factors such as temperature, feeding frequency, and the type of flour used. At warmer temperatures, yeast activity increases, producing more carbon dioxide and faster rising. At cooler temperatures, bacterial activity dominates, producing more acid and a tangier flavor. The starter must be maintained by regular feeding — typically every 12 to 24 hours at room temperature — to keep the microbial population healthy and active. When added to bread dough, the starter not only leavens the bread but also improves its texture, extends its shelf life, and makes nutrients more bioavailable by breaking down gluten and phytic acid.
